full_prose_under_review.title: Restricted Sales Without a Prescription: Scheduled Listed Chemical Products, Excepted Controlled-Substance Preparations and Hypodermic Syringes
full_prose_under_review.topic: Restricted nonprescription products / Selling without a prescription under federal and Massachusetts law
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: The federal retail rules for scheduled listed chemical products in 21 U.S.C. 830(d) and (e), 21 U.S.C. 844(a) and 21 CFR part 1314 - who and what they reach, the calendar-day, mobile-vendor, mail-order and purchaser 30-day limits, nonliquid packaging, behind-the-counter placement and delivery, the logbook and purchaser identification with the single-package 60 mg exception, sales-personnel training, self-certification and its fee, logbook disclosure and privacy, the prohibited acts in 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) that reach a seller's employees and agents, loss reporting and the effect on State law - and the absence, as of September 16, 2026, of added requirements in M.G.L. c. 94C, 247 CMR and 105 CMR 700.000; the route in M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 4 and 5 for selling an excepted controlled-substance preparation, the absence as of September 16, 2026 of any s. 4 exception in the regulations searched, the federal exclusion and exemption categories in 21 U.S.C. 811(g) on which s. 4(3) depends, and 21 CFR 1306.26 read with the prescription requirement of s. 17(c); and the sale of hypodermic syringes and needles under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 27 as amended by chapter 208 of the Acts of 2018, the s. 32I(d) carve-out, the point-of-sale educational insert in M.G.L. c. 111, s. 25K and the Board's advisory

orientation.text: Two kinds of product can be sold in a Massachusetts pharmacy without a prescription and still cannot be handled as ordinary merchandise, and a third route, for controlled-substance preparations, appears in the statutes but is not open today. Products containing ephedrine, pseudoephedrine or phenylpropanolamine that may lawfully be marketed as nonprescription drugs are scheduled listed chemical products, and their retail sale is governed by federal law: 21 U.S.C. 830(d) and (e), the purchase prohibition in 21 U.S.C. 844(a) and 21 CFR part 1314. Hypodermic syringes and needles are governed by Massachusetts law, centrally M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 27. A controlled-substance preparation could be sold at retail under Massachusetts law only through M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 5, which reaches only a preparation excepted by regulation under s. 4, and as of September 16, 2026 no such exception appears in the Department's or the Board's regulations described below; the section explains why that route is closed, what federal law provides in 21 CFR 1306.26 where it reaches a nonprescription sale, and why Massachusetts law keeps that federal route closed too. Three neighbouring subjects lie outside this section and are only named here: which drugs sit in which schedule, the opioid antagonist and other standing-order routes to dispensing without an individual prescription, and dispensing on a prescription.

Part 1314 states its own reach. It specifies the requirements for retail sales of scheduled listed chemical products to individuals for personal use (21 CFR 1314.01). Its subpart B applies to regulated sellers, whose sales are face-to-face sales at stores or by mobile retail vendors, and its subpart C applies to regulated persons who ship the products to the customer by the U.S. Postal Service or by private or common carriers (21 CFR 1314.02). A mail-order sale is one in which a regulated person uses or attempts to use the Postal Service or a private or commercial carrier to deliver the product to the customer, including orders submitted by phone, mail, fax, Internet or any method other than a face-to-face transaction (21 CFR 1314.03). Under 21 CFR 1300.02 a scheduled listed chemical product is a product that contains ephedrine, pseudoephedrine or phenylpropanolamine, including their salts, optical isomers and salts of optical isomers, and that may be marketed or distributed lawfully in the United States under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as a nonprescription drug; a product that is a controlled substance under part 1308 is not one. A regulated seller is a retail distributor, including a pharmacy or a mobile retail vendor, and the term does not include an employee or agent of the distributor. The duties described below are therefore placed on the pharmacy as the seller, and the employees who hand over the product or take payment for it must have received the training the seller gives and certifies. Employees are not beyond the Act's reach, however: 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) makes it unlawful for a regulated seller or an employee or agent of the seller to disclose logbook information in violation of the privacy regulations, or to refuse to provide the logbook to Federal, State or local law enforcement authorities.

As of September 16, 2026, none of M.G.L. c. 94C, the Board's regulations in 247 CMR or the Department's controlled substances regulation, 105 CMR 700.000, addresses scheduled listed chemical products or adds a quantity limit, age limit, logbook or other retail requirement for them. The federal part leaves room for State law on the same subject: nothing in part 1314 preempts State law on the same subject matter unless there is a positive conflict so that the two cannot consistently stand together (21 CFR 1314.10), and a record developed and maintained to comply with a State law may be used to meet the federal logbook requirement if it includes the information the federal section specifies (21 CFR 1314.30(h)). Measured against those Massachusetts provisions, the retail requirements for these products are the federal requirements set out in this section.

The quantity rules are the part of the scheme most often misattributed, because the familiar figures bind different parties over different periods. A regulated seller, including a mobile retail vendor, may not in a single calendar day sell any purchaser more than 3.6 grams of ephedrine base, 3.6 grams of pseudoephedrine base or 3.6 grams of phenylpropanolamine base in scheduled listed chemical products, and the limit applies without regard to the number of transactions (21 CFR 1314.20(a); 21 U.S.C. 830(d)(1)). Every figure is stated in grams of base, not in the weight of the product or a count of tablets. A mobile retail vendor carries a second ceiling of not more than 7.5 grams of any of those bases to an individual purchaser in any 30-day period (21 CFR 1314.20(b)), and the mail-order limits in 21 CFR 1314.100 hold a regulated person whose retail sales must be reported under 21 CFR 1310.03(c) to 3.6 grams per purchaser in a calendar day and 7.5 grams per individual purchaser in any 30-day period. The 9-gram figure does not appear in 21 CFR 1314.20 at all. It comes from 21 U.S.C. 844(a), which makes it unlawful for any person to knowingly or intentionally purchase at retail during a 30 day period more than 9 grams of ephedrine base, pseudoephedrine base or phenylpropanolamine base in a scheduled listed chemical product, and of those 9 grams not more than 7.5 grams may be imported by shipping through a private or commercial carrier or the Postal Service. The 9-gram limit is a prohibition on the purchaser; for a regulated seller that is neither a mobile retail vendor nor subject to the mail-order limits, the federal quantity limit is the calendar-day limit.

Before any logbook is opened, the product itself must be packaged, placed and handed over in a prescribed way. A regulated seller or mail order distributor may not sell a scheduled listed chemical product in nonliquid form, including gel caps, unless it is packaged in blister packs with each blister containing no more than two dosage units or, if blister packs are technically infeasible, in unit dose packets or pouches (21 CFR 1314.05; 21 U.S.C. 830(d)(2)). The seller must place the product so that customers do not have direct access to it before the sale is made. That behind-the-counter placement includes storage in a locked cabinet located in an area of the facility where customers do have direct access, and a mobile retail vendor must place the product in a locked cabinet (21 CFR 1314.25(b)). The seller must then deliver the product directly into the custody of the purchaser (21 CFR 1314.25(c)). Each regulated seller must ensure that its retail sales of these products are made in accordance with those requirements and with the quantity limits of 21 CFR 1314.20 (21 CFR 1314.25(a)).

The logbook is the documentary core of the scheme. Except for a purchase by an individual of a single sales package containing not more than 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine, the regulated seller must maintain a written or electronic list of each sale that identifies the products by name, the quantity sold, the names and addresses of the purchasers and the dates and times of the sales (21 CFR 1314.30(a)). The statute ties the identification and signature steps to that same logbook requirement, applying them in the case of a sale to which the logbook requirement applies (21 U.S.C. 830(e)(1)(A)(iv)), so the single-package exception reaches the identification check as well as the logbook entry. The exception is narrow three times over: it is limited to pseudoephedrine, to one sales package and to a package containing not more than 60 milligrams. For every other face-to-face sale the purchaser presents an identification card that provides a photograph and is issued by a State or the Federal Government, or a document acceptable for purposes of 8 CFR 274a.2(b)(1)(v)(A) and (B), and signs the logbook, and the seller enters the name of the product and the quantity sold. If the purchaser enters the name, address, date and time, the seller must determine that the name entered corresponds to the name on the identification and that the date and time are correct; if the seller enters them, the prospective purchaser must verify that they are correct (21 CFR 1314.30(b) and (c)).

The regulation also fixes how the logbook is signed, what it warns, where it is kept and who may see it. With a written logbook the purchaser signs by entering his name, address and the date and time of the sale; with an electronic logbook the purchaser signs a device presented by the seller that captures the signature electronically and displays the warning notice, or a bound paper book carrying a printed sticker or unique identifier linked to the sale, or a printed document produced by the seller at the time of sale and placed in a binder or other secure storage immediately after signing (21 CFR 1314.30(b)(2)). The logbook, or a display by it, must carry the notice that under 18 U.S.C. 1001 knowingly and willfully falsifying the logbook or making a materially false statement in it is punishable by a fine of not more than $250,000 for an individual or $500,000 for an organization, imprisonment of not more than five years, or both (21 CFR 1314.30(d)). Each entry is maintained for not fewer than two years after the date on which it is made (21 CFR 1314.30(e)). Records are kept at the place of business where the transaction occurred unless the seller has notified the Administration, by written notification sent by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, to the Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Divisional Office for the area, that it will keep them at a single central location, and they must be readily retrievable and available for inspection and copying by authorized DEA employees (21 CFR 1314.30(f) and (g)). Logbook information shall be disclosed as appropriate to the Administration and to State and local law enforcement agencies, the information in the logbooks shall not be accessed, used or shared for any purpose other than ensuring compliance or facilitating a product recall to protect public health and safety, and a regulated seller that releases it in good faith to Federal, State or local law enforcement authorities is immune from civil liability unless the release constitutes gross negligence or intentional, wanton or willful misconduct (21 CFR 1314.45(a)-(c)). Those rules are backed by a prohibition that is not confined to the seller: under 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) it is unlawful for a regulated seller or an employee or agent of the seller to disclose logbook information in violation of the privacy regulations, or to refuse to provide the logbook to Federal, State or local law enforcement authorities. A violation carries a civil penalty under 21 U.S.C. 842(c)(1)(A), and it is a crime under 842(c)(2) only if it is prosecuted as, and specifically found to have been, committed knowingly.

No sale may be made until the seller's own standing with DEA is in place. The individuals who deliver the products into purchasers' custody, or who deal directly with purchasers by obtaining payment for the products, must have undergone training provided by the regulated seller, in accordance with criteria issued by the Administration, so that they understand the requirements of part 1314, and the seller must have submitted to the Administration a self-certification that all such individuals have been trained (21 CFR 1314.35(a)). A regulated seller must submit that self-certification in order to sell any scheduled listed chemical product, and the certification is not effective unless it also states that the seller understands each of the requirements of the part and agrees to comply with them (21 CFR 1314.40(a)). A separate certification is required for each place of business at which the seller sells these products at retail (21 CFR 1314.40(c)), so a certification held for one store does not reach another. When the initial certification is filed, DEA assigns the seller to one of twelve groups whose certifications expire on the last day of the group's designated month, at a date not less than 12 or more than 23 months after the certification, and after that initial period the seller must update the self-certification annually (21 CFR 1314.40(b)). The fee is $21 for each initial self-certification and each renewal, paid by credit card at the time of self-certification and not refundable, and it is waived for any person holding a current DEA registration in good standing as a pharmacy to dispense controlled substances (21 CFR 1314.42). The seller keeps a copy of each self-certification and all records demonstrating that the individuals have been trained (21 CFR 1314.35(b)).

Two further federal provisions complete the seller's side. Each regulated person must report any unusual or excessive loss or disappearance of a scheduled listed chemical product under its control to the Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Divisional Office for the area in which it is located: orally, whenever possible, at the earliest practicable opportunity after it becomes aware of the circumstances, and in a written report filed within 15 days after it becomes aware of them, describing the circumstances of the loss; for a loss in transit, the supplier is the one responsible for reporting (21 CFR 1314.15). And a regulated seller may take reasonable measures to guard against employing individuals who may present a risk of theft and diversion of these products, which may include, notwithstanding State law, asking applicants for employment whether they have been convicted of any crime involving or related to such products or controlled substances (21 CFR 1314.50).

The Massachusetts route for selling a controlled-substance preparation at retail begins with a gate that is easy to overlook. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 4 the commissioner, acting jointly with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, may by regulation under chapter 30A except a compound, mixture or preparation containing substances in paragraph (a) or (b) of Schedule III or in Schedule IV, V or VI from the application of all or any part of chapter 94C, if three conditions are all met: the preparation contains one or more active medicinal ingredients not having a depressant or stimulant effect on the central nervous system; those ingredients are included in such combinations, quantity, proportion or concentration as to vitiate the potential for abuse of the substances that do have such an effect; and the preparation has been similarly excepted under the federal Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970. The regulation must state the weight of the controlled substance per fluid ounce, or the corresponding avoirdupois or metric weight, and the commissioner must by regulation modify, rescind or revoke an exception whenever the federal exception is modified, rescinded or revoked. An exception is therefore a regulatory act about a particular preparation. A product's place in Schedule V, or its federal marketing as a nonprescription drug, is not itself a s. 4 exception. As of September 16, 2026, no regulation excepting any preparation under s. 4 appears in the Department's regulation 105 CMR 700.000, in the Department's other drug regulations at 105 CMR 720.000, 721.000, 722.000, 724.000 and 726.000, or in any chapter of the Board's regulations in 247 CMR. Within 105 CMR 700.000, section 105 CMR 700.002 establishes Schedules I through V as the substances listed in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 and Schedule VI as all prescription drugs not included in another schedule, and it states no exception. Section 5 therefore has, at present, no excepted preparation to apply to.

The third condition in s. 4 ties any exception to federal law, and federal law limits what could be excepted. Under 21 U.S.C. 811(g)(1) a non-narcotic drug containing a controlled substance that may lawfully be sold over the counter without a prescription is to be excluded by regulation from the application of the federal Act, and under 811(g)(3) a preparation can be exempted only if it is a nonnarcotic preparation approved for prescription use whose unscheduled active ingredients vitiate the potential for abuse, a preparation not for administration to a human being or animal that as packaged presents no significant potential for abuse, or, on the recommendation of the Secretary of Health and Human Services, an anabolic steroid preparation that presents no significant potential for abuse; DEA's provisions on excluded and exempted substances and preparations are at 21 CFR 1308.21 to 1308.35. A nonprescription preparation containing opium, which 21 U.S.C. 802(17) makes a narcotic drug, fits none of those categories, so as federal law now stands it could not satisfy s. 4(3), and no regulation could except it under s. 4.

Section 5 states the terms that would govern a preparation if one were excepted under s. 4: it may be dispensed, or sold at retail, subject to conditions. The preparation must be dispensed or sold in good faith as a medicine and not for the purpose of evading the provisions of the controlled substances law; the purchaser must identify himself to the satisfaction of the pharmacist; and not more than four ounces may be dispensed or sold to a person during any 48 hour period. The pharmacist dispensing such excepted substances must keep an accurate record book including the name and address of the purchaser, the name of the preparation, the strength per dosage unit, the quantity dispensed and the date. Three features of the text are worth holding exactly. The identification standard is the pharmacist's satisfaction rather than a listed document, and s. 5 states no minimum age. The four-ounce ceiling runs per person over any 48 hour period, not per transaction or per calendar day. And the section speaks throughout of the pharmacist, a word chapter 94C defines as any pharmacist registered in the commonwealth to dispense controlled substances, including any other person authorized to dispense controlled substances under the supervision of a pharmacist registered in the commonwealth.

Federal law sets a separate list of conditions wherever it reaches a nonprescription sale of a controlled substance. Under 21 CFR 1306.26 a controlled substance listed in Schedule II, III, IV or V that is not a prescription drug under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act may be dispensed by a pharmacist without a prescription to a purchaser at retail, provided that: the dispensing is made only by a pharmacist and not by a nonpharmacist employee, even under a pharmacist's supervision, although once the pharmacist has fulfilled those responsibilities a nonpharmacist may complete the cash or credit transaction or the delivery; not more than 240 cc (8 ounces) or 48 dosage units of a controlled substance containing opium, nor more than 120 cc (4 ounces) or 24 dosage units of any other, is dispensed to the same purchaser in any given 48-hour period; the purchaser is at least 18 years of age; every purchaser not known to the pharmacist furnishes suitable identification, including proof of age where appropriate; the pharmacist maintains a bound record book with the purchaser's name and address, the name and quantity of the controlled substance, the date of each purchase and the name or initials of the dispensing pharmacist, kept under the recordkeeping requirement of 21 CFR 1304.04, which requires records to be kept and available for inspection for at least two years; and a prescription is not required for the distribution or dispensing of the substance under any other Federal, State or local law. A central fill pharmacy may not dispense under the section at all. For these purposes a pharmacist, as defined in 21 CFR 1300.01, includes any other person, such as a pharmacist intern, authorized by a State to dispense controlled substances under the supervision of a pharmacist licensed by that State.

Read together, these provisions settle what happens when a customer in Massachusetts asks for a controlled-substance preparation without a prescription. Massachusetts provides that a controlled substance included in Schedule III, IV, V or VI shall not be dispensed without an electronic prescription from a practitioner (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c)), subject to exceptions that allow a written or oral prescription instead, and s. 5, the provision of chapter 94C that allows a controlled substance to be sold at retail, reaches only preparations excepted under s. 4, of which the regulations described above contain none. The condition in 21 CFR 1306.26(f) that no other Federal, State or local law require a prescription is therefore not met, so federal law does not open a nonprescription sale on its own, and the request is declined. The federal and Massachusetts terms are still worth keeping apart, because they differ on several points: the four-ounce ceiling in s. 5 against the federal 240 cc and 120 cc volume caps and 48 and 24 dosage-unit caps; the federal minimum age of 18, dispensing by the pharmacist rather than a nonpharmacist employee, the bar on central fill pharmacies and the pharmacist's name or initials in the bound record book, which s. 5 does not state; and good faith as a medicine and the strength per dosage unit, which the federal section does not state. That comparison is a comparison of texts. It does not describe a sale that can be made in Massachusetts today, and for a nonprescription preparation containing opium it could not describe one while s. 4(3) and 21 U.S.C. 811(g) stand as they do.

Hypodermic syringes and needles are governed by a single sentence. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 27, hypodermic syringes or hypodermic needles for the administration of controlled substances by injection may be sold in the commonwealth only by a pharmacist or wholesale druggist licensed under chapter 112, a manufacturer of or dealer in surgical supplies, or a manufacturer of or dealer in embalming supplies. The section's operative condition is who sells: it states no prescription requirement, no minimum age, no identification requirement, no quantity limit and no record. Only the age and identification points changed in 2018. The text of s. 27 enacted by chapter 172 of the Acts of 2006 already dealt with sales made without a prescription and set no quantity limit or record, but it limited sales to persons who have attained the age of 18 years and required a pharmacist or wholesale druggist selling without a prescription to require proof of identification that validates the individual's age; chapter 208 of the Acts of 2018 struck both. Two other statutes attach to the sale. The drug paraphernalia offense in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 32I does not apply to the sale of hypodermic syringes or hypodermic needles pursuant to s. 27 (s. 32I(d)). And M.G.L. c. 111, s. 25K directs the Department to develop an educational insert covering the proper use of syringes and needles, the risk of blood-borne diseases and methods of preventing them, proper disposal practices, and the toll-free numbers of the commonwealth's AIDS and Hepatitis C hotlines and the Massachusetts Substance Abuse Information and Education Helpline, and provides that the insert shall be provided to purchasers of hypodermic syringes or needles at the point of sale. That sentence is passive and does not name who provides the insert; the course that is safe on any reading is for the seller to hand it over with each sale.

The Board's advisory on the sale of hypodermic syringes and needles, first adopted on December 6, 2016, reads s. 27 as authorizing pharmacies to sell hypodermic syringes and needles to any person, of any age, without a prescription and without identification, and observes that the legislation does not limit the number or type of syringes and needles that may be sold to any one customer. Its recommendations are guidance rather than regulation, and they are worded that way: the pharmacy should complete the sale without any further requirements or record keeping; there is no need to restrict the quantity or type, such as IM syringes; it is strongly recommended that the pharmacy stock single unit-of-use syringes for individual sale; and pharmacies may provide information on proper use and disposal. That permissive wording on information does not displace the statutory sentence in M.G.L. c. 111, s. 25K that the Department's insert shall be provided at the point of sale. One question the texts leave open is who within a store may make the sale: s. 27 names categories of seller and says nothing about their employees, while the advisory speaks of the pharmacy completing the sale. Where the register is not staffed as part of the pharmacy, the course that is safe on either reading is to route the sale through the pharmacist.
