worked_examples.scenario: At 10 a.m. a customer buys packages of a nonprescription decongestant containing 2.4 grams of pseudoephedrine base in total at a Massachusetts pharmacy, presenting a state driver's licence and signing the logbook. At 4 p.m. he returns to the same pharmacy for another package containing 1.8 grams of pseudoephedrine base and mentions that he bought 6 grams of pseudoephedrine base at another store nine days earlier. The employee at the register reasons that the afternoon purchase is a separate transaction, that only the 9-gram limit could matter, and that Massachusetts must have its own limit the pharmacy should check instead.
steps: Identify the limit that binds the pharmacy. Under 21 CFR 1314.20(a) a regulated seller may not in a single calendar day sell any purchaser more than 3.6 grams of pseudoephedrine base in scheduled listed chemical products, and the limit applies without regard to the number of transactions.

Add the day's sales to this purchaser: 2.4 grams in the morning and 1.8 grams in the afternoon would come to 4.2 grams, which is more than 3.6 grams, so the afternoon package cannot be sold however the sale is rung up.

Place the 9-gram figure correctly. It is the prohibition in 21 U.S.C. 844(a) on any person purchasing at retail more than 9 grams during a 30 day period; with 6 grams bought nine days earlier and 2.4 grams bought this morning, the customer is already at 8.4 grams, so a further purchase of more than 0.6 grams within that period would be his own violation of 844(a).

Check for a Massachusetts layer. As of September 16, 2026, none of M.G.L. c. 94C, 247 CMR or 105 CMR 700.000 adds a quantity limit for these products, so the federal calendar-day limit is the limit the pharmacy applies.

Keep the transaction requirements in view for any sale that does go ahead: the product stays behind the counter, is delivered directly into the purchaser's custody, and is entered in the logbook after the purchaser presents acceptable identification and signs.
worked_examples.resolution: The afternoon package may not be sold, because it would take the pharmacy's sales to that purchaser to 4.2 grams in one calendar day, over the 3.6-gram limit that applies whatever the number of transactions. The error the scenario invites is treating the purchaser's 9-gram 30-day prohibition as the only limit, and looking for a Massachusetts limit that none of chapter 94C, 247 CMR or 105 CMR 700.000 contains.

worked_examples.scenario: A traveller who has no identification document with him asks a Massachusetts pharmacy for one sales package containing 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine. Behind him, a second customer who also has no acceptable identification asks for two packages of the same product, 120 milligrams in all, and points out that each package would qualify on its own.
steps: Read the exception in the regulation. Under 21 CFR 1314.30(a) the logbook requirement does not apply to a purchase by an individual of a single sales package containing not more than 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine.

Read how the statute attaches identification. 21 U.S.C. 830(e)(1)(A)(iv) applies the identification and signature requirements in the case of a sale to which the logbook requirement applies, so the traveller's single-package purchase needs neither a logbook entry nor identification.

Keep the rest of the scheme in place for the first sale: the package is sold from behind-the-counter placement, delivered directly into the purchaser's custody, counted toward the 3.6-gram calendar-day limit, and sold by a seller that has self-certified.

Test the second request against the words of the exception. Two packages are not a purchase of a single sales package, so the logbook requirement applies, and under 21 CFR 1314.30(b) the seller must not sell unless the purchaser presents a photographic identification card issued by a State or the Federal Government, or a document acceptable under 8 CFR 274a.2(b)(1)(v)(A) and (B), and signs the logbook.
worked_examples.resolution: The traveller's single 60-milligram package may be sold without a logbook entry or identification, but the second customer's two packages may not be sold without acceptable identification and a signed logbook entry, even though together they contain only 120 milligrams. The error the scenario invites is reading the exception as a low-quantity allowance rather than an exception for one package of pseudoephedrine.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy company that holds a current DEA pharmacy registration in good standing has self-certified its first Massachusetts store and trained that store's staff. It opens a second store across town, moves two trained employees there and hires a new cashier. The district manager plans to put a pseudoephedrine product on an open aisle display beside the pharmacy counter, to rely on the first store's certificate, and to let the new cashier take payment for these products before completing training.
steps: Start with the certification unit. Under 21 CFR 1314.40(c) a regulated seller must provide a separate certification for each place of business at which it sells scheduled listed chemical products at retail, and under 1314.40(a) it must submit the self-certification in order to sell, so the first store's certificate does not authorize sales at the second.

Check who must be trained. The self-certification attests that every individual who delivers the products into purchasers' custody or deals directly with purchasers by obtaining payment has undergone the seller's training (21 CFR 1314.35(a)), so the new cashier must be trained before taking payment for these products, and the certification is not effective unless it states that the seller understands the requirements and agrees to comply (1314.40(a)).

Settle the fee. The $21 fee for each self-certification is waived for any person holding a current DEA registration in good standing as a pharmacy to dispense controlled substances (21 CFR 1314.42(b)); the waiver removes only the fee, and the certification is still required.

Correct the display. An open aisle display gives customers direct access to the product before the sale, which 21 CFR 1314.25(b) does not allow; the product must be placed behind the counter or in a locked cabinet, which may stand in an area customers can reach.

Note the renewal cycle and the records. DEA assigns the initial certification to a group expiring not less than 12 or more than 23 months out, after which the seller must update the self-certification annually (21 CFR 1314.40(b)), and the seller keeps a copy of each certification and the training records (1314.35(b)).
worked_examples.resolution: The second store may not sell until it has its own self-certification, the new cashier must be trained before taking payment for these products, no fee is due for a seller holding a current DEA pharmacy registration in good standing, and the product must move behind the counter or into a locked cabinet. The error the scenario invites is treating one store's certification as covering the company, and treating the fee waiver as a waiver of certification.

worked_examples.scenario: A 17-year-old asks a Massachusetts pharmacist to sell him, without a prescription, six fluid ounces of a liquid preparation that is a Schedule V controlled substance containing opium and is marketed federally as a nonprescription drug. He says he will be back the next morning for the same amount. The pharmacist believes that federal law allows up to 8 ounces of such a preparation in 48 hours and that nothing more needs to be checked.
steps: Begin with Massachusetts. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) a controlled substance in Schedule V shall not be dispensed without an electronic prescription from a practitioner, and s. 5, the chapter 94C route for a retail sale, reaches only a preparation excepted under s. 4.

Look for a s. 4 exception. An exception is made only by regulation of the commissioner acting jointly with the Board, and neither the preparation's place in Schedule V nor its federal nonprescription marketing is such a regulation. As of September 16, 2026 no regulation excepting any preparation under s. 4 appears in 105 CMR 700.000, 720.000, 721.000, 722.000, 724.000 or 726.000 or in 247 CMR, so s. 5 does not reach this sale.

Ask whether an exception could be made for this product. Section 4(3) requires that the preparation have been similarly excepted under the federal Act, and a nonprescription preparation containing opium, a narcotic drug under 21 U.S.C. 802(17), fits neither the exclusion in 21 U.S.C. 811(g)(1), which is limited to non-narcotic drugs, nor any exemption category in 811(g)(3), so as federal law now stands it could not be excepted.

Test the federal route against its own terms. 21 CFR 1306.26(f) makes the nonprescription route depend on no other Federal, State or local law requiring a prescription, and s. 17(c) requires one, so the federal 240 cc allowance for a preparation containing opium never applies here; even where the federal route is open, 1306.26(c) requires a purchaser at least 18 years of age.
worked_examples.resolution: No sale can be made without a prescription, to this purchaser or to an adult: the preparation is a Schedule V controlled substance that s. 17(c) requires a prescription to dispense, no s. 4 exception brings it within s. 5, none could be made for it while federal law stands as it does, and 21 CFR 1306.26 does not apply while State law requires a prescription. The error the scenario invites is treating the federal 8-ounce figure as a permission that applies in Massachusetts on its own.

worked_examples.scenario: A 16-year-old with no identification asks for a box of 100 hypodermic syringes with needles at the front register of a Massachusetts drugstore that contains a pharmacy. The register clerk, who works for the store rather than the pharmacy department, proposes to ask for identification, to limit the sale to ten syringes, to write the sale in a log, and to leave out any leaflet because the Board's advisory says pharmacies may provide use and disposal information.
steps: Identify the permitted sellers. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 27 hypodermic syringes or needles for the administration of controlled substances by injection may be sold only by a pharmacist or wholesale druggist licensed under chapter 112, a manufacturer of or dealer in surgical supplies, or a manufacturer of or dealer in embalming supplies. The section says nothing about the seller's employees, and the Board's advisory speaks of the pharmacy completing the sale, so the course that is safe on either reading is to route this sale through the pharmacist.

Remove the conditions the law no longer contains. Chapter 208 of the Acts of 2018 struck the age-18 limit and the proof-of-age identification requirement from s. 27, and the Board's advisory reads s. 27 as allowing sales to any person, of any age, without a prescription and without identification.

Drop the quantity cap and the log. Section 27 states no quantity limit or record, and the Board advises that there is no need to restrict the quantity or type and that the pharmacy should complete the sale without any further requirements or record keeping.
Set aside the paraphernalia concern. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 32I(d) the paraphernalia offense does not apply to the sale of hypodermic syringes or hypodermic needles pursuant to s. 27.

Restore the insert. M.G.L. c. 111, s. 25K provides that the Department's educational insert shall be provided to purchasers of hypodermic syringes or needles at the point of sale; the advisory's statement that pharmacies may provide use and disposal information does not displace that sentence, so the insert goes with the sale.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist may sell the 16-year-old the full box without identification, a quantity cap or a record, and the Department's educational insert is to be provided with it. The error the scenario invites is applying the age and identification conditions that were struck from s. 27 in 2018, and reading the Board's permissive wording on information as if it replaced the statutory insert.

worked_examples.scenario: A local police detective asks a Massachusetts pharmacy manager for every logbook entry naming a particular purchaser. The same week the chain proposes to move all of its logbooks to a regional office, and the manager finds that a sealed case of a pseudoephedrine product has disappeared from the stockroom, a loss the manager regards as unusual. The manager asks whether the entries may be shown to the detective, whether entries made 26 months ago still have to be kept, whether the move needs any step first, and whether the missing case must be reported.
steps: Disclosure. Under 21 CFR 1314.45(a) logbook information shall be disclosed as appropriate to the Administration and to State and local law enforcement agencies, so a local detective's request is one the regulation provides for; under 1314.45(b) the information may not be accessed, used or shared for any other purpose than compliance or a product recall; and under 1314.45(c) a regulated seller that releases it in good faith to Federal, State or local law enforcement authorities is immune from civil liability unless the release constitutes gross negligence or intentional, wanton or willful misconduct. The manager is an employee, and 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) makes it unlawful for the seller or an employee or agent of the seller to refuse to provide the logbook to Federal, State or local law enforcement authorities, or to disclose its information in violation of the privacy regulations.
Retention. Each entry must be maintained for not fewer than two years after the date on which it is made (21 CFR 1314.30(e)), so entries made 26 months ago are past the federal minimum period.

Location. Records are kept at the place of business where the transaction occurred unless the seller has notified the Administration of its intention to keep them at a single central location, by written notification sent by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, to the Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Divisional Office for the area in which the records are required to be kept (21 CFR 1314.30(f)); wherever kept, they must be readily retrievable and available for DEA inspection and copying (1314.30(g)).

Loss. An unusual or excessive loss or disappearance of a scheduled listed chemical product under the seller's control is reported to the Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Divisional Office for the area: orally whenever possible at the earliest practicable opportunity after the seller becomes aware of it, and in writing within 15 days after becoming aware, with a description of the circumstances (21 CFR 1314.15).
worked_examples.resolution: The entries are to be disclosed to the detective as appropriate, and refusing to provide the logbook would be a prohibited act for the pharmacy and for the manager personally; entries more than two years old are past the federal retention minimum, the move to a central location needs the written notification to DEA first, and the missing case calls for an oral report as soon as practicable and a written report within 15 days after the manager became aware of it. The error the scenario invites is treating the logbook as a private business record the pharmacy may decline to share, treating employees as outside the federal logbook rules, and treating a stock disappearance as a purely internal inventory matter.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A regulated seller may not sell any purchaser more than ______ grams of pseudoephedrine base in a single ______, and the limit applies without regard to ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 3.6; calendar day; the number of transactions, under 21 CFR 1314.20(a).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where does the 9-gram figure come from, and whom does it bind?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 21 U.S.C. 844(a). It makes it unlawful for any person to knowingly or intentionally purchase at retail during a 30 day period more than 9 grams of ephedrine base, pseudoephedrine base or phenylpropanolamine base in a scheduled listed chemical product, so it binds the purchaser; it is not stated in 21 CFR 1314.20.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which sellers carry a 30-day limit, and what is it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A mobile retail vendor, which may not sell an individual purchaser more than 7.5 grams of any of the bases in any 30-day period under 21 CFR 1314.20(b), and a regulated person whose retail sales must be reported under 21 CFR 1310.03(c), which is held to the same 7.5 grams and to 3.6 grams per calendar day under 21 CFR 1314.100.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a customer may buy two 60-milligram packages of pseudoephedrine without a logbook entry because each package qualifies for the single-package exception.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The exception in 21 CFR 1314.30(a) covers a purchase by an individual of a single sales package containing not more than 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine; a purchase of two packages requires the logbook entry and, under 21 U.S.C. 830(e)(1)(A)(iv), the identification and signature.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What identification satisfies the federal retail requirement for a sale that needs a logbook entry?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An identification card that provides a photograph and is issued by a State or the Federal Government, or a document acceptable for purposes of 8 CFR 274a.2(b)(1)(v)(A) and (B), under 21 CFR 1314.30(b)(1).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long is a logbook entry kept, and where?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Not fewer than two years after the date on which the entry is made, at the place of business where the transaction occurred or, if the seller has notified DEA in writing by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, at a single central location (21 CFR 1314.30(e) and (f)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Must logbook information be given to State and local law enforcement, and who can commit the prohibited act in 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Under 21 CFR 1314.45(a) the information shall be disclosed as appropriate to DEA and to State and local law enforcement agencies. 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) makes it unlawful for a regulated seller or an employee or agent of the seller to disclose logbook information in violation of the privacy regulations, or to refuse to provide the logbook to Federal, State or local law enforcement authorities.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must the logbook warning notice state?
retrieval_prompts.answer: That under 18 U.S.C. 1001 knowingly and willfully falsifying the logbook or making materially false statements in it is punishable by a fine of not more than $250,000 for an individual or $500,000 for an organization, imprisonment of not more than five years, or both (21 CFR 1314.30(d)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the placement and delivery requirements for a regulated seller.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Customers must not have direct access to the product before the sale, with a locked cabinet in a customer-accessible area counting as behind-the-counter placement and a locked cabinet required of a mobile retail vendor, and the seller must deliver the product directly into the custody of the purchaser (21 CFR 1314.25(b) and (c)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How must a nonliquid scheduled listed chemical product be packaged?
retrieval_prompts.answer: In blister packs with no more than two dosage units in each blister or, if blister packs are technically infeasible, in unit dose packets or pouches (21 CFR 1314.05).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a pharmacy chain's self-certification covers every store it operates.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 21 CFR 1314.40(c) requires a separate certification for each place of business at which the seller sells scheduled listed chemical products at retail.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What is the self-certification fee, and who does not pay it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: $21 for each initial self-certification and each renewal, paid by credit card at the time of self-certification and not refundable; it is waived for any person holding a current DEA registration in good standing as a pharmacy to dispense controlled substances (21 CFR 1314.42).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Whom must a regulated seller train before selling scheduled listed chemical products?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Every individual who is responsible for delivering the products into the custody of purchasers or who deals directly with purchasers by obtaining payment for the products (21 CFR 1314.35(a)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: When is the written report of an unusual or excessive loss of a scheduled listed chemical product due, and who reports a loss in transit?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Within 15 days after the regulated person becomes aware of the circumstances, following an oral report made whenever possible at the earliest practicable opportunity; the supplier reports a loss in transit (21 CFR 1314.15).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Do M.G.L. c. 94C, 247 CMR or 105 CMR 700.000 add retail requirements of their own for pseudoephedrine products?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. As of September 16, 2026, none of them addresses scheduled listed chemical products, so the federal requirements govern the sale; under 21 CFR 1314.10, part 1314 does not preempt State law on the same subject unless the two cannot consistently stand together.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 5, how much of an excepted preparation may be dispensed or sold to a person, and over what period?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Not more than four ounces during any 48 hour period.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: List the items the s. 5 record book must include.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The name and address of the purchaser, the name of the preparation, the strength per dosage unit, the quantity dispensed and the date.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must be true of a preparation before s. 5 applies to it?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It must have been excepted under s. 4 by regulation of the commissioner acting jointly with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, and it can be excepted only if it contains one or more active medicinal ingredients not having a depressant or stimulant effect on the central nervous system, in combinations, quantity, proportion or concentration that vitiate the potential for abuse, and has been similarly excepted under the federal Act.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: As of September 16, 2026, can a Massachusetts pharmacy sell any controlled-substance preparation at retail under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 5?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. No regulation excepting a preparation under s. 4 appears in 105 CMR 700.000, 720.000, 721.000, 722.000, 724.000 or 726.000 or in 247 CMR, so s. 5 has no excepted preparation to apply to, and s. 17(c) requires a prescription to dispense a Schedule III, IV, V or VI controlled substance.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why could a nonprescription preparation containing opium not be excepted under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 4 as federal law now stands?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Section 4(3) requires that the preparation have been similarly excepted under the federal Act. The exclusion in 21 U.S.C. 811(g)(1) is limited to non-narcotic drugs, and 811(g)(3) allows exemptions only for a nonnarcotic preparation approved for prescription use, a preparation not for administration to a human being or animal, and certain anabolic steroid preparations; a preparation containing opium is a narcotic drug under 21 U.S.C. 802(17) and fits none of these.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 21 CFR 1306.26, what is the minimum purchaser age, and who may do the dispensing?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 18 years. The dispensing is made only by a pharmacist, which 21 CFR 1300.01 defines to include a person such as a pharmacist intern authorized by a State to dispense under a licensed pharmacist's supervision, and not by a nonpharmacist employee; a nonpharmacist may complete the cash or credit transaction or the delivery afterwards.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why does 21 CFR 1306.26 not by itself allow a Schedule V preparation to be sold without a prescription in Massachusetts?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because 21 CFR 1306.26(f) applies only where no other Federal, State or local law requires a prescription, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) requires one to dispense a Schedule V controlled substance; the Massachusetts route for a retail sale is s. 5, which reaches only a preparation excepted under s. 4, and as of September 16, 2026 no preparation is excepted.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may sell hypodermic syringes and needles for the administration of controlled substances by injection in Massachusetts?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A pharmacist or wholesale druggist licensed under chapter 112, a manufacturer of or dealer in surgical supplies, or a manufacturer of or dealer in embalming supplies (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 27).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Must a purchaser of hypodermic syringes in Massachusetts be 18 or show identification?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Chapter 208 of the Acts of 2018 struck both the age-18 limit and the proof-of-age identification requirement from M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 27, and the Board's advisory reads s. 27 as allowing sales to any person, of any age, without a prescription and without identification.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must be provided to purchasers of hypodermic syringes or needles at the point of sale?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The educational insert the Department develops under M.G.L. c. 111, s. 25K, covering proper use, the risk of blood-borne diseases and methods of preventing them, proper disposal, and the toll-free numbers of the commonwealth's AIDS and Hepatitis C hotlines and the Massachusetts Substance Abuse Information and Education Helpline.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does the drug paraphernalia offense reach a pharmacist's sale of hypodermic needles under s. 27?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 32I(d) provides that s. 32I does not apply to the sale of hypodermic syringes or hypodermic needles pursuant to s. 27.

quick_review.text: Scheduled listed chemical products are nonprescription products containing ephedrine, pseudoephedrine or phenylpropanolamine; their retail sale is governed by 21 U.S.C. 830(d) and (e), 21 U.S.C. 844(a) and 21 CFR part 1314.

A pharmacy is a regulated seller and its employees and agents are not, but 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) reaches them too: disclosing logbook information in violation of the privacy regulations, or refusing the logbook to law enforcement, is unlawful for the seller and for its employees and agents.
As of September 16, 2026, M.G.L. c. 94C, 247 CMR and 105 CMR 700.000 add no retail requirements for these products, and 21 CFR 1314.10 leaves consistent State law in place.

The seller's limit is 3.6 grams of base per purchaser per calendar day, whatever the number of transactions; mobile retail vendors and sellers subject to the mail-order limits are also held to 7.5 grams per individual purchaser in any 30-day period.
The 9-gram 30-day figure is the purchaser prohibition in 21 U.S.C. 844(a), and not more than 7.5 grams of it may be shipped.
Nonliquid forms go in blister packs of no more than two dosage units per blister, or in unit dose packets or pouches if blister packs are technically infeasible.
The product is placed where customers have no direct access before the sale, or in a locked cabinet, and is delivered directly into the purchaser's custody.

Every face-to-face retail sale needs a logbook entry, listed identification and the purchaser's signature, except an individual's purchase of a single sales package containing not more than 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine.

Logbook entries are kept not fewer than two years after they are made, at the place of business or, after written notice to DEA, at a central location, and the logbook carries the 18 U.S.C. 1001 warning.
Logbook information shall be disclosed as appropriate to DEA and to State and local law enforcement, and is otherwise accessed, used or shared only for compliance or a product recall.

Each place of business self-certifies before selling, the seller trains everyone who delivers the product or takes payment and keeps the records, and the certification is updated annually after the initial period.
The $21 self-certification fee is waived for a person holding a current DEA registration in good standing as a pharmacy to dispense controlled substances.
An unusual or excessive loss is reported to DEA orally at the earliest practicable opportunity whenever possible and in writing within 15 days after the seller becomes aware of it.

Massachusetts lets a controlled-substance preparation be sold at retail under s. 5 only if a regulation under s. 4 has excepted it, and as of September 16, 2026 no such regulation appears in 105 CMR 700.000, the Department's other drug regulations or 247 CMR, so no such sale is currently available.

If a preparation were ever excepted under s. 4, s. 5 would require good faith as a medicine, identification to the pharmacist's satisfaction, not more than four ounces to a person in any 48 hour period, and a record book.
Section 4(3) needs a federal exception, and no federal exclusion or exemption category in 21 U.S.C. 811(g) fits a nonprescription preparation containing opium.

21 CFR 1306.26 requires dispensing by a pharmacist, a purchaser of at least 18, 48-hour volume and dosage-unit caps and a bound record book, bars central fill pharmacies, and applies only where no other law requires a prescription.
Massachusetts requires an electronic prescription to dispense a Schedule III, IV, V or VI substance under s. 17(c), so federal permission alone does not open a nonprescription sale here.

Hypodermic syringes and needles for injecting controlled substances may be sold only by a pharmacist or wholesale druggist licensed under chapter 112 or a manufacturer of or dealer in surgical or embalming supplies.

Since the 2018 amendments s. 27 carries no age or identification condition, s. 32I(d) keeps s. 27 sales outside the paraphernalia offense, and s. 25K requires the Department's insert to be provided at the point of sale.
The Board advises completing syringe sales without further requirements or record keeping and strongly recommends stocking single unit-of-use syringes.

decision_logic.condition: A customer asks for a product containing ephedrine, pseudoephedrine or phenylpropanolamine.
decision_logic.action: Confirm that it is a scheduled listed chemical product, a product that may lawfully be marketed as a nonprescription drug and is not itself a controlled substance, and apply the federal retail requirements of 21 CFR part 1314 and 21 U.S.C. 830 and 844(a); as of September 16, 2026, M.G.L. c. 94C, 247 CMR and 105 CMR 700.000 add none.

decision_logic.condition: A store is about to make its first sale of these products.
decision_logic.action: Check that this place of business has its own self-certification on file with DEA, that every individual who will deliver the product or take payment has been trained, and that the certification copy and training records are kept; the $21 fee is payable unless the seller holds a current DEA registration in good standing as a pharmacy to dispense controlled substances.

Keep nonliquid forms in blister packs of no more than two dosage units, or unit dose packets or pouches where blister packs are technically infeasible, and place the products where customers cannot reach them before the sale or in a locked cabinet.

decision_logic.condition: The customer wants one sales package containing not more than 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine and nothing else.
decision_logic.action: The sale needs no logbook entry or identification, but it is still made from behind-the-counter placement, delivered directly into the purchaser's custody and counted toward the calendar-day limit.

decision_logic.condition: A face-to-face purchase is anything other than a single sales package of not more than 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine.
decision_logic.action: Require photographic identification issued by a State or the Federal Government, or a document acceptable under 8 CFR 274a.2(b)(1)(v)(A) and (B); have the purchaser sign; enter the product and quantity; and verify the name, date and time as 21 CFR 1314.30(c) directs. Without acceptable identification, do not sell.

decision_logic.condition: The purchaser has already bought these products from this seller today.
decision_logic.action: Add the day's sales of each base to the request; if the total would exceed 3.6 grams, the sale may not be made however it is divided into transactions.

decision_logic.condition: The purchaser mentions other purchases within the past 30 days.
decision_logic.action: Treat the 9-gram figure as the purchaser's own prohibition under 21 U.S.C. 844(a); the pharmacy's quantity limit remains the calendar-day limit unless it is a mobile retail vendor or subject to the mail-order limits.

decision_logic.condition: Stock disappears, or law enforcement asks for logbook entries.
decision_logic.action: Report an unusual or excessive loss to the DEA Special Agent in Charge for the area orally at the earliest practicable opportunity whenever possible and in writing within 15 days after becoming aware. Disclose logbook information as appropriate to DEA and to State and local law enforcement, as 21 CFR 1314.45(a) requires, bearing in mind that refusing to provide the logbook to Federal, State or local law enforcement is unlawful for the seller and for its employees and agents under 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14); use the information for no purpose other than compliance or a product recall.

decision_logic.condition: A customer asks to buy a controlled-substance preparation, such as a Schedule V preparation, without a prescription.
decision_logic.action: Do not sell it on s. 5 or 21 CFR 1306.26 terms. As of September 16, 2026 no regulation under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 4 excepts any preparation, so s. 5 does not apply, and s. 17 requires a prescription to dispense a controlled substance in Schedules II through VI, so 21 CFR 1306.26(f) is not met either; routes such as dispensing under a standing order are outside this section.

decision_logic.condition: A regulation under s. 4 is adopted in future excepting a preparation (none exists as of September 16, 2026).
decision_logic.action: Apply s. 5: good faith as a medicine, identification to the pharmacist's satisfaction, not more than four ounces to the person in any 48 hour period, and a record book entry with the purchaser's name and address, the preparation, the strength per dosage unit, the quantity and the date.

decision_logic.condition: Someone asks to buy hypodermic syringes or needles.
decision_logic.action: Make the sale through a seller s. 27 names, in a pharmacy the pharmacist, without asking age or identification, without a quantity cap and without a record, and provide the Department's educational insert at the point of sale.

ma_vs_federal.text: Scheduled listed chemical products: federal law supplies the retail requirements. As of September 16, 2026, none of M.G.L. c. 94C, 247 CMR or 105 CMR 700.000 addresses these products, and 21 CFR 1314.10 provides that part 1314 does not preempt State law on the same subject matter unless the two cannot consistently stand together.

Controlled-substance preparations sold without a prescription: the terms of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 5 and 21 CFR 1306.26 differ, since the four-ounce ceiling in s. 5 stands against the federal volume and dosage-unit caps, and the federal minimum age of 18, pharmacist dispensing and central fill bar have no counterpart in s. 5. Neither opens a sale in Massachusetts today: as of September 16, 2026 no regulation under s. 4 excepts any preparation, so s. 5 has nothing to apply to, and 21 CFR 1306.26(f) is not met while s. 17 requires a prescription. Nor could the two sets of terms meet in one sale of a nonprescription preparation containing opium, since s. 4(3) requires a federal exception that 21 U.S.C. 811(g) does not provide for it.

The federal nonprescription route depends on State law: 21 CFR 1306.26(f) requires that no other Federal, State or local law require a prescription, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) requires one to dispense a Schedule III, IV, V or VI substance.

Records: the s. 5 record book must include the strength per dosage unit, which the federal bound record book does not list, while the federal book must include the dispensing pharmacist's name or initials and is kept under 21 CFR 1304.04 for at least two years. Section 5 states no retention period of its own, but M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 15 requires persons registered to dispense controlled substances to keep records in conformance with the federal record-keeping requirements and with any additional rules of the Board.

Who counts as a pharmacist: 21 CFR 1300.01 includes any other person, such as a pharmacist intern, authorized by a State to dispense controlled substances under the supervision of a licensed pharmacist, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 includes any other person authorized to dispense controlled substances under the supervision of a pharmacist registered in the commonwealth.
Hypodermic syringes and needles: the sale terms taught here are Massachusetts terms, set by M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 27 and 32I(d) and M.G.L. c. 111, s. 25K, with the Board's advisory as guidance.

exceptions.text: A purchase by an individual of a single sales package containing not more than 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine needs no logbook entry, and the statute attaches identification and signature only to sales that need one.
Under 21 U.S.C. 830(e)(1)(F) the retail-transaction requirements of 830(e)(1)(A) do not apply to a sale whose transaction must be reported under 830(b)(3); such sales are subject to 830(e)(2).
Behind-the-counter placement includes storing the product in a locked cabinet located in an area of the facility where customers do have direct access.
Where blister packs are technically infeasible, nonliquid forms may be packaged in unit dose packets or pouches.
The $21 self-certification fee is waived for any person holding a current DEA registration in good standing as a pharmacy to dispense controlled substances; the certification itself is not waived.
Logbook records may be kept at a single central location instead of the place of business where the transaction occurred, once the seller has given DEA the required written notification.
A record developed and maintained to comply with a State law may serve as the federal logbook if it includes the information 21 CFR 1314.30 specifies.

A regulated seller may, notwithstanding State law, ask applicants for employment whether they have been convicted of any crime involving or related to scheduled listed chemical products or controlled substances.
Of the 9 grams a person may purchase at retail during a 30 day period, not more than 7.5 grams may be imported by shipping through a private or commercial carrier or the Postal Service.
For a loss of a scheduled listed chemical product in transit, the supplier is the regulated person responsible for reporting.
Under 21 CFR 1306.26 a nonpharmacist may complete the cash or credit transaction or the delivery after the pharmacist has fulfilled the pharmacist's responsibilities.

A regulation under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 4 may except a preparation from the application of all or any part of chapter 94C; as of September 16, 2026 no such regulation appears in 105 CMR 700.000, the Department's other drug regulations or 247 CMR.
M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 32I does not apply to the sale of hypodermic syringes or hypodermic needles pursuant to s. 27.

timing_deadlines.event: Sales of scheduled listed chemical products to one purchaser
timing_deadlines.consequence: Not more than 3.6 grams of ephedrine base, pseudoephedrine base or phenylpropanolamine base, without regard to the number of transactions.

timing_deadlines.event: Sales by a mobile retail vendor, or by a seller subject to the mail-order limits, to one individual purchaser
timing_deadlines.consequence: Not more than 7.5 grams of any of those bases.

timing_deadlines.event: A person's retail purchases of these products
timing_deadlines.consequence: Purchasing more than 9 grams of any of those bases is unlawful under 21 U.S.C. 844(a), and not more than 7.5 grams of the 9 may be shipped.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not fewer than two years after the date of the entry
timing_deadlines.consequence: The entry must be maintained, readily retrievable and available for DEA inspection and copying throughout that period.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Expires on the last day of the month designated for the assigned group, not less than 12 or more than 23 months after certification
timing_deadlines.consequence: After the initial certification period the seller must update the self-certification annually.

timing_deadlines.event: The seller becomes aware of an unusual or excessive loss or disappearance
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Orally at the earliest practicable opportunity, whenever possible; in writing within 15 days after becoming aware
timing_deadlines.consequence: The report goes to the DEA Special Agent in Charge for the area and describes the circumstances of the loss.

timing_deadlines.event: Sales of an excepted preparation to one person under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 5
timing_deadlines.consequence: Not more than four ounces may be dispensed or sold; the ceiling would apply only to a preparation excepted under s. 4, and none is excepted as of September 16, 2026.

timing_deadlines.event: Nonprescription dispensing to the same purchaser under 21 CFR 1306.26
timing_deadlines.consequence: Not more than 240 cc or 48 dosage units of a controlled substance containing opium, or 120 cc or 24 dosage units of any other.

timing_deadlines.event: A purchase is entered in the 21 CFR 1306.26 bound record book
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least two years, under 21 CFR 1304.04
timing_deadlines.consequence: The record must be kept and available for inspection for that period.

timing_deadlines.event: A federal exception on which a s. 4 exception rests is modified, rescinded or revoked
timing_deadlines.consequence: The commissioner shall by regulation modify, rescind or revoke the Massachusetts exception.

timing_deadlines.event: Sale of hypodermic syringes or needles
timing_deadlines.consequence: The Department's educational insert shall be provided to the purchaser under M.G.L. c. 111, s. 25K.

forms_records.text: The logbook is a written or electronic list of each sale identifying the products by name, the quantity sold, the names and addresses of the purchasers and the dates and times of the sales; the purchaser's signature and the seller's entry of the product and quantity complete each entry.

An electronic logbook is signed on a device that captures signatures electronically and displays the warning notice, in a bound paper book carrying a printed sticker or unique identifier linked to the sale, or on a document printed at the time of sale and placed in a binder or other secure storage immediately after signing.

The 18 U.S.C. 1001 warning notice, stating a fine of not more than $250,000 for an individual or $500,000 for an organization and imprisonment of not more than five years, appears in the logbook or is displayed by it.

Keeping logbook records at a single central location requires written notification to the Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Divisional Office for the area, sent by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested.
A record kept to comply with a State law may serve as the federal logbook if it includes the information 21 CFR 1314.30 specifies.

The self-certification, filed with DEA for each place of business, attests to the training of every individual who delivers the product or takes payment and states that the seller understands the requirements and agrees to comply; the seller keeps a copy of each certification.
The seller keeps all records demonstrating that the individuals who deliver the product or take payment for it have undergone the training.

A loss report is made orally whenever possible and filed in writing within 15 days after the seller becomes aware of the loss, describing its circumstances such as loss in transit or theft from the premises; 21 CFR 1314.15 provides a suggested format.

The s. 5 record book, kept by the pharmacist dispensing excepted substances, includes the purchaser's name and address, the name of the preparation, the strength per dosage unit, the quantity dispensed and the date; it would be needed only for a preparation excepted under s. 4, and none is excepted as of September 16, 2026.

The 21 CFR 1306.26 bound record book, maintained by the pharmacist, contains the purchaser's name and address, the name and quantity of controlled substance purchased, the date of each purchase and the name or initials of the dispensing pharmacist, and is kept under 21 CFR 1304.04 for at least two years.

A sale of hypodermic syringes or needles under s. 27 carries no statutory record, and the Board advises completing it without record keeping; the document the law does require is the Department's educational insert, provided at the point of sale.

role_duties.duty: Observe the 3.6-gram calendar-day limit, package nonliquid forms as required, keep the product behind the counter or locked, deliver it directly into the purchaser's custody, maintain the logbook with identification and signature for every face-to-face retail sale outside the single-package exception, keep each entry two years, disclose logbook information as appropriate to DEA and to State and local law enforcement and use it for no other purpose than compliance or a product recall, and report unusual or excessive losses.

Train every individual who delivers the product or takes payment for it, self-certify each place of business with the statement of understanding and agreement, pay the fee unless it holds a current DEA pharmacy registration in good standing, keep the certification and training records, and update the certification annually after the initial period.

role_duties.role: Employee or agent of a retail distributor
role_duties.duty: Is not a regulated seller, but must not disclose logbook information in violation of the privacy regulations or refuse to provide the logbook to Federal, State or local law enforcement authorities, both of which 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) makes unlawful for an employee or agent as well as for the seller; an employee responsible for delivering the product or taking payment for it must have received the seller's training.
Keep the product in a locked cabinet, and sell no individual purchaser more than 7.5 grams of any of the bases in any 30-day period in addition to observing the calendar-day limit.

role_duties.role: Regulated person subject to the mail-order limits
role_duties.duty: Sell no purchaser more than 3.6 grams of any of the bases in a calendar day and no individual purchaser more than 7.5 grams in any 30-day period.

role_duties.role: Purchaser of a scheduled listed chemical product
role_duties.duty: Present acceptable identification and sign the logbook for any purchase other than a single sales package of not more than 60 milligrams of pseudoephedrine, and not purchase at retail more than 9 grams of any of the bases in a 30 day period.

role_duties.role: Supplier of scheduled listed chemical products
role_duties.duty: Report a loss of the products in transit.

Receive self-certifications and assign each initial certification to one of twelve groups expiring not less than 12 or more than 23 months out, and receive loss reports and notices of central logbook record-keeping.

role_duties.role: Commissioner of public health acting jointly with the Board of Registration in Pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Except a preparation by regulation under s. 4 only where its three conditions are met, stating the weight of the controlled substance as s. 4 directs.
Modify, rescind or revoke a s. 4 exception by regulation whenever the federal exception has been modified, rescinded or revoked.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist, if a preparation is ever excepted under s. 4
role_duties.duty: Under s. 5, be satisfied of the purchaser's identity, sell in good faith as a medicine, keep to four ounces per person in any 48 hour period, and keep the record book; as of September 16, 2026 no preparation is excepted, so no sale is made on these terms.

Where no other Federal, State or local law requires a prescription, do the dispensing, confirm that the purchaser is at least 18, require suitable identification from purchasers not known to the pharmacist, observe the 48-hour volume and dosage-unit caps, and maintain the bound record book; in Massachusetts s. 17(a) and (c) require a prescription for a controlled substance in Schedules II through VI, so the route is not available there.

role_duties.role: Nonpharmacist employee in a 21 CFR 1306.26 sale
role_duties.duty: May complete the cash or credit transaction or the delivery only after the pharmacist has fulfilled the pharmacist's responsibilities, and may not do the dispensing.
May not dispense controlled substances to a purchaser at retail under 21 CFR 1306.26.

role_duties.role: Seller of hypodermic syringes and needles
role_duties.duty: Be a pharmacist or wholesale druggist licensed under chapter 112 or a manufacturer of or dealer in surgical or embalming supplies and, as the safe course under s. 25K, provide the Department's educational insert at the point of sale.
Develop the educational insert that accompanies the sale of hypodermic syringes and needles.

Advises that pharmacies complete syringe and needle sales without further requirements or record keeping and without restricting quantity or type, and strongly recommends stocking single unit-of-use syringes.

common_traps.text: Treating 9 grams as the pharmacy's limit. The 9-gram 30-day figure is the purchaser prohibition in 21 U.S.C. 844(a); it does not appear in 21 CFR 1314.20.
Resetting the daily limit with each transaction. The 3.6-gram limit runs per purchaser per calendar day without regard to the number of transactions.
Measuring the limits by product weight or tablet count. Every quantity figure is stated in grams of base.
Reading the 60-milligram exception as a low-dose allowance. It covers only an individual's purchase of a single sales package of pseudoephedrine containing not more than 60 milligrams.
Stopping at the quantity limits. A sale within the limits still needs the logbook entry, identification and signature unless the single-package exception applies.

Treating logbook disclosure to law enforcement as optional, or employees as outside the federal logbook rules. Logbook information shall be disclosed as appropriate to DEA and to State and local law enforcement, and 21 U.S.C. 842(a)(14) makes unlawful disclosure, or refusing to provide the logbook to law enforcement, a prohibited act for the seller's employees and agents as well as for the seller.
Treating a certification as company-wide. Each place of business at which the seller sells these products at retail needs its own certification.
Treating training and self-certification as alternatives, or the fee waiver as a certification waiver. The certification attests to the training, and the pharmacy waiver removes only the $21 fee.
Leaving the product on an open shelf near the pharmacy. Customers must have no direct access before the sale unless the product is in a locked cabinet.

Looking for a Massachusetts pseudoephedrine limit, age limit or logbook in chapter 94C or the Board's or the Department's regulations. As of September 16, 2026, M.G.L. c. 94C, 247 CMR and 105 CMR 700.000 contain none, so the federal requirements govern.

Treating a product's Schedule V placement or federal nonprescription marketing as a s. 4 exception. Only a regulation of the commissioner acting jointly with the Board makes one, and as of September 16, 2026 no such regulation appears in 105 CMR 700.000, the Department's other drug regulations or 247 CMR.

Assuming a new Massachusetts regulation could except a nonprescription preparation containing opium. Section 4(3) requires a federal exception, and no federal exclusion or exemption category in 21 U.S.C. 811(g) fits such a preparation.

Applying the federal 8-ounce figure in Massachusetts. No controlled-substance preparation can be sold here on s. 5 or 21 CFR 1306.26 terms today: with no s. 4 exception, s. 17 requires a prescription, and the four-ounce ceiling in s. 5 would matter only for a preparation excepted in future.
Letting a nonpharmacist employee make a 21 CFR 1306.26 sale. The pharmacist does the dispensing; a nonpharmacist may only complete the cash or credit transaction or the delivery afterwards.
Requiring a syringe purchaser to be 18 or to show identification. Chapter 208 of the Acts of 2018 struck both conditions from s. 27.

Reading the Board's statement that pharmacies may provide use and disposal information as the whole of the insert duty. M.G.L. c. 111, s. 25K provides that the Department's insert shall be provided at the point of sale.
Treating the Board's syringe recommendations as legal requirements. Completing the sale without further requirements and stocking single unit-of-use syringes are recommended actions in guidance.

drug_examples.teaching_point: A nonprescription pseudoephedrine decongestant is a scheduled listed chemical product rather than a controlled substance: its retail sale runs on the federal calendar-day limit, blister packaging for nonliquid forms, behind-the-counter placement, the logbook and identification, and the seller's self-certification, and the 60-milligram exception applies only to a single sales package of pseudoephedrine.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 21 CFR part 1314 specifies the requirements for retail sales of scheduled listed chemical products to individuals for personal use (1314.01). It applies to regulated sellers of scheduled listed chemical products sold at retail for personal use through face-to-face sales at stores or mobile retail vendors, and to regulated persons who engage in a transaction with a non-regulated person and ship the products by the U.S. Postal Service or by private or common carriers; the requirements of subpart A apply to all regulated persons subject to the part, those of subpart B to regulated sellers as defined in 21 CFR 1300.02, and those of subpart C to regulated persons who ship the products to the customer by the U.S. Postal Service or by private or common carriers (1314.02). A mail-order sale is a retail sale of scheduled listed chemical products for personal use where a regulated person uses or attempts to use the U.S. Postal Service or any private or commercial carrier to deliver the product to the customer, and includes purchase orders submitted by phone, mail, fax, Internet, or any method other than a face-to-face transaction (1314.03). Under 21 CFR 1300.02, a scheduled listed chemical product is a product that contains ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, or phenylpropanolamine (including their salts, optical isomers, and salts of optical isomers) and may be marketed or distributed lawfully in the United States under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as a nonprescription drug, and the term does not include any product that is a controlled substance under part 1308; a regulated seller is a retail distributor (including a pharmacy or a mobile retail vendor), except that the term does not include an employee or agent of the distributor; a retail distributor is a grocery store, general merchandise store, drug store, or other entity or person whose activities as a distributor relating to drug products containing ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, or phenylpropanolamine are limited almost exclusively to sales for personal use, both in number of sales and volume of sales, either directly to walk-in customers or in face-to-face transactions by direct sales; and a mobile retail vendor is a person or entity that makes sales at retail from a stand that is intended to be temporary or is capable of being moved from one location to another. Under 21 U.S.C. 830(e)(1)(F), the retail-transaction requirements of 830(e)(1)(A) do not apply to the sale at retail of a scheduled listed chemical product if a report on the sales transaction is required to be submitted under 830(b)(3). Under 21 CFR 1314.10, nothing in part 1314 preempts State law on the same subject matter unless there is a positive conflict between the part and a State law so that the two cannot consistently stand together.
exceptions: Under 21 U.S.C. 830(e)(1)(F), the retail-transaction requirements of 830(e)(1)(A) do not apply to a retail sale for which a report on the sales transaction is required under 830(b)(3); such sales are subject to 830(e)(2).

authority.name: Regulation of listed chemicals and certain machines

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1314.20(a) and 21 U.S.C. 830(d)(1), without regard to the number of transactions, a regulated seller (including a mobile retail vendor) may not in a single calendar day sell any purchaser more than 3.6 grams of ephedrine base, 3.6 grams of pseudoephedrine base, or 3.6 grams of phenylpropanolamine base in scheduled listed chemical products. Under 21 CFR 1314.20(b) and 21 U.S.C. 830(e)(1)(A)(ix)(II), a mobile retail vendor may not in any 30-day period sell an individual purchaser more than 7.5 grams of ephedrine base, 7.5 grams of pseudoephedrine base, or 7.5 grams of phenylpropanolamine base in scheduled listed chemical products. Under 21 CFR 1314.100, headed sales limits for mail-order sales, and 21 U.S.C. 830(d)(1) and (e)(2)(B), each regulated person who makes a sale at retail of a scheduled listed chemical product and is required under 21 CFR 1310.03(c) to submit a report of the sales transaction may not in a single calendar day sell to any purchaser more than 3.6 grams, and may not in any 30-day period sell to an individual purchaser more than 7.5 grams, of ephedrine base, pseudoephedrine base, or phenylpropanolamine base in scheduled listed chemical products. 21 CFR 1314.20 states no 30-day limit for a regulated seller that is not a mobile retail vendor. Separately, 21 U.S.C. 844(a) makes it unlawful for any person to knowingly or intentionally purchase at retail during a 30 day period more than 9 grams of ephedrine base, pseudoephedrine base, or phenylpropanolamine base in a scheduled listed chemical product, except that, of such 9 grams, not more than 7.5 grams may be imported by means of shipping through any private or commercial carrier or the Postal Service.
exceptions: Of the 9 grams a person may purchase at retail during a 30 day period, not more than 7.5 grams may be imported by means of shipping through any private or commercial carrier or the Postal Service.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 4, the commissioner acting jointly with the board of registration in pharmacy may by regulation pursuant to chapter 30A except any compound, mixture or preparation containing any substances in paragraph (a) or (b) of Schedule III or in Schedule IV, V or VI from the application of all or any part of chapter 94C if (1) the compound, mixture, or preparation contains one or more active medicinal ingredients not having a depressant or stimulant effect on the central nervous system, (2) such ingredients are included therein in such combinations, quantity, proportion, or concentration as to vitiate the potential for abuse of the substances which do have a depressant or stimulant effect on the central nervous system, and (3) the compound, mixture, or preparation has been similarly excepted under the federal Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970 or any amendment of it. Such a regulation shall state the weight of the controlled substance per fluid ounce, or if a solid or semi-solid preparation the weight in the avoirdupois amounts, and if the metric system is used, the weight in grams per hundred cubic centimeters for a fluid or the weight per gram for a solid or semi-solid preparation, and the commissioner shall by regulation modify, rescind or revoke an exception whenever it has been modified, rescinded or revoked under the federal Act. Under s. 5, controlled substances which are excepted pursuant to s. 4 may be dispensed, or sold at retail, subject to the conditions (1) that the preparation is dispensed, or sold in good faith as a medicine, and not for the purpose of evading the provisions of the controlled substances law; (2) that the purchaser of the preparation identify himself to the satisfaction of the pharmacist; and (3) that not more than four ounces of the preparation are dispensed, or sold to a person during any 48 hour period; and the pharmacist dispensing such excepted substances shall keep an accurate record book including the name and address of the purchaser, the name of the preparation, the strength per dosage unit, the quantity dispensed and the date. Section 1 of chapter 94C defines pharmacist as any pharmacist registered in the commonwealth to dispense controlled substances, and including any other person authorized to dispense controlled substances under the supervision of a pharmacist registered in the commonwealth. No other section of chapter 94C refers to a controlled substance being sold at retail. 105 CMR 700.002 establishes Schedules I through V as the drugs and other substances listed in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 and Schedule VI as all prescription drugs not included in any other schedule, and neither 105 CMR 700.000 nor 247 CMR 2.00 through 21.00 states an exception under s. 4.
exceptions: A regulation under s. 4 may except a preparation from the application of all or any part of chapter 94C.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.26, a controlled substance listed in Schedules II, III, IV, or V which is not a prescription drug as determined under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act may be dispensed by a pharmacist without a prescription to a purchaser at retail, provided that: (a) such dispensing is made only by a pharmacist, as defined in part 1300, and not by a nonpharmacist employee even if under the supervision of a pharmacist, although after the pharmacist has fulfilled his professional and legal responsibilities set forth in the section the actual cash, credit transaction, or delivery may be completed by a nonpharmacist; (b) not more than 240 cc. (8 ounces) of any such controlled substance containing opium, nor more than 120 cc. (4 ounces) of any other such controlled substance, nor more than 48 dosage units of any such controlled substance containing opium, nor more than 24 dosage units of any other such controlled substance may be dispensed at retail to the same purchaser in any given 48-hour period; (c) the purchaser is at least 18 years of age; (d) the pharmacist requires every purchaser of a controlled substance under the section not known to him to furnish suitable identification (including proof of age where appropriate); (e) a bound record book for dispensing of controlled substances under the section is maintained by the pharmacist, containing the name and address of the purchaser, the name and quantity of controlled substance purchased, the date of each purchase, and the name or initials of the pharmacist who dispensed the substance to the purchaser, and the book is maintained in accordance with the recordkeeping requirement of 21 CFR 1304.04; and (f) a prescription is not required for distribution or dispensing of the substance pursuant to any other Federal, State or local law. Under 1306.26(g), central fill pharmacies may not dispense controlled substances to a purchaser at retail pursuant to the section. 21 CFR 1300.01 defines pharmacist as any pharmacist licensed by a State to dispense controlled substances, including any other person (e.g., pharmacist intern) authorized by a State to dispense controlled substances under the supervision of a pharmacist licensed by such State.
exceptions: After the pharmacist has fulfilled the pharmacist's professional and legal responsibilities under 21 CFR 1306.26, the actual cash, credit transaction, or delivery may be completed by a nonpharmacist.
